idiom_name: one stage type per step + single implementation + private constructor + terminal build()
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: declare one small type (interface, protocol, trait or struct) per step whose only members are that step's operations and whose methods return the next stage's type; implement them all in one non-public builder that accumulates the partially built product; keep the product's constructor and the first stage behind a single public entry point so callers cannot start mid-sequence; declare build()/the product conversion only on the final stage. Validate cross-field rules once in the terminal step, and decide deliberately how optional groups are modelled - a self-returning final stage, or a final stage that extends the optional interface, so repeatable calls stay available without re-opening the required steps.
code_sketch:
entry() -> Step1                 # the only way in
Step1.op(a) -> Step2             # each stage returns the next stage
Step2.op(b) -> Step3             # build() is not visible yet
Step3.op?(c) -> Step3            # repeatable optional steps stay on Step3
Step3.build() -> Product         # terminal step: validate, then construct
pitfalls: Publishing the implementation type or a public constructor lets callers enter the chain anywhere and defeats the staging.
Repeatable optional operations need the final stage to extend the optional interface; otherwise a second optional call is unavailable and callers append it in the wrong place.
The chain can only express sequences known statically; a next step chosen from run-time data must branch outside the staged types.

Wrong move: implementing the stages as one public generic type with phantom markers (Builder<HasUrl, HasBody>) -> callers name that type in variables and a skipped step surfaces as an unsatisfied trait bound naming types they never wrote -> instead expose named per-stage types that hide the markers, and (in Rust) add diagnostic hints, since sled's API guidance warns that typestate violations 'often lack specificity' in their error messages.

Wrong move: giving every single property its own interface in one fixed mandatory order -> adding a property later, or demoting one to optional, rewrites the stage chain and breaks every existing call site -> instead group stages by domain phase and prefer an order-preserving staged style (e.g. Jilt's STAGED_PRESERVING_ORDER) so optional properties can be skipped without breaking callers.

Wrong move: staging construction wherever correctness is merely nice-to-have because compile-time enforcement is elegant -> N stage types, harder-to-document typestate friction and a wider diff on every field change for no prevented incident -> instead reserve the staging for sequences whose misuse is expensive (sled's guidance: weigh typestate friction in non-correctness-critical components) and use named/defaulted arguments elsewhere.
